script.opening: "This sounds odd, doctor. For two weeks me, my partner and the two kids have all had headaches, felt sick and dizzy and tired — even the dog seems off and sleepy. We feel rough at home, especially mornings, but when we’re out for the day we’re fine. Is there a bug going round?"

facts.text: At home, in the lounge, on the phone. Has a headache now and feels "a bit woozy". The two children (9 and 6) are at school; partner, Lee, is at work. The dog is in the kitchen.

Two weeks. Dull headache, nausea, dizziness, tiredness — all four of them. Worse first thing in the morning and in the evenings. Better within an hour or two of going out. Weekend at her mum’s: all felt fine.
Nobody has collapsed, fitted or been confused. No chest pain or breathlessness. Nobody pregnant. The 6-year-old was sick twice last week.

Old terraced house, rented. Gas boiler in the kitchen and a gas fire in the lounge that they’ve had on a lot since the cold weather started. Noticed some black sooty marks around the gas fire. Doesn’t think there’s a carbon monoxide alarm. Doesn’t know when the boiler was last serviced — the landlord deals with it.
All generally healthy. Gemma takes no medicines. Smokes about 5 a day outside.

Puzzled, chatty at first. When the doctor suggests carbon monoxide, become frightened: "Are you serious?" Follow instructions if they are clear (go outside with the dog). Feel guilty — "I’ve had the kids in there. Have I made them ill?" Ask "Couldn’t I just check them with one of those finger oxygen monitors?" and "When can we go back home?"

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — once CO is mentioned: guilt — "Have I poisoned my children?" Also worried about the landlord and money if they have to leave the house.
ice.expectations: "Something for the bug, or to be told it’ll pass."

cues: "Even the dog seems off" — everyone in the house, including the pet.
"When we’re out for the day we’re fine" — the home-related pattern.
"Have I made them ill?" — guilt to address while giving clear emergency instructions.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the CARBON MONOXIDE pattern — flu-like symptoms in MULTIPLE household members (and pets), worse at home (mornings/heating), improving away — not labelling it a virus
Asks about the COMBUSTION SOURCE (gas boiler/fire/cooker, solid-fuel stove, blocked/faulty flue, ventilation) and whether a CO alarm is present
Gives IMMEDIATE emergency advice — everyone (and pets) OUT into fresh air, turn off the appliance, ventilate, call the National Gas Emergency Service (0800 111 999)/999 — without delay

Arranges urgent MEDICAL assessment, knowing treatment is high-flow O2, carboxyhaemoglobin supports exposure (but a normal level taken late or after oxygen does not exclude it; smokers’ baseline is higher), and hyperbaric decisions follow NPIS/TOXBASE advice
Knows pulse OXIMETRY reads FALSELY NORMAL in CO poisoning and is not falsely reassured by normal sats

Advises PREVENTION — CO alarms, appliance/flue servicing by a registered engineer, ventilation, no unsuitable appliances indoors, landlord duties if rented — and review for delayed neurological effects
Connects the pattern for the patient and conveys urgency clearly without panic, ensuring she acts immediately
Arranges disposition: immediate evacuation + gas emergency/999, urgent assessment for those affected, prevention advice, escalation if anyone drowsy/unconscious

worked.txt: "This doesn’t sound like a bug. All of you — and the dog — feeling ill at home, worse mornings with the heating on, and fine when out, is the classic pattern of carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty appliance. This is urgent."
"Act now: get everyone and the dog OUT into fresh air. If safe, turn off the boiler/fire and open windows on your way out. Don’t stay inside."

"From outside, call the gas emergency line on 0800 111 999 — they’ll check the property urgently — and if anyone is drowsy, confused or very unwell, call 999. CO can be dangerous quickly, especially overnight."

"You all need assessment today — the treatment is high-flow oxygen, and a blood test can show it, although the level falls once you’re out in fresh air, so a normal result later doesn’t rule it out. Importantly, the finger oxygen monitors read normal even when CO is high, so don’t be falsely reassured by that."

"Once safe, get a CO alarm fitted and have the boiler, gas appliances and flue checked by a registered Gas Safe engineer before using them again. If you rent, your landlord has to arrange the gas safety check and alarms. And let me know if anyone has memory, concentration or mood problems in the coming weeks."
"So: out into fresh air now, gas emergency line, 999 if anyone’s drowsy or faints. Don’t go back until it’s declared safe. Ring me once you’re all out and I’ll help arrange check-ups."

f.learning: CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) POISONING is recognised by non-specific FLU-LIKE symptoms — headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, sometimes confusion — affecting MULTIPLE PEOPLE and PETS in the SAME HOME, WORSE at home (mornings/heating on) and IMPROVING when AWAY; CO is the "great mimic", commonly misdiagnosed as a viral illness, migraine or food poisoning, so the household + pet + home-related + improves-away pattern is the crucial clue. Ask about the combustion source (gas boiler/fire/cooker, solid-fuel stove, blocked/faulty flue, poor ventilation, unserviced appliance) and a CO alarm. The immediate action is an EMERGENCY: get everyone (and pets) OUT into fresh air, turn off the appliance if safe, ventilate, don’t stay inside, and call the National Gas Emergency Service (0800 111 999) and 999/urgent assessment — CO can rapidly cause loss of consciousness and death, particularly overnight. Arrange urgent assessment: treatment is high-flow 100% OXYGEN (speeds CO elimination), a raised carboxyhaemoglobin level supports exposure (but it falls once away from the source and faster on oxygen, so a normal level taken late does not exclude it, and smokers have higher baseline levels), and hyperbaric oxygen decisions for severe cases (neuro signs, LOC, pregnancy, cardiac involvement) follow NPIS/TOXBASE advice. Critically, pulse OXIMETRY reads FALSELY NORMAL because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin — a normal sats reading is misleadingly reassuring. Advise prevention: CO alarms, servicing by a registered (Gas Safe) engineer, ventilation, and no unsuitable appliances (BBQs/generators) indoors; landlords must arrange annual gas safety checks and CO alarms; and review for delayed neurological effects. The skill is recognising the pattern, immediate emergency advice, assessment without false reassurance from oximetry, and prevention — not labelling it viral.

knowledge.guideline: [1] UKHSA Carbon monoxide: general information (GOV.UK) · [2] UKHSA Carbon monoxide: toxicological overview (GOV.UK) · [3] National Gas Emergency Service (0800 111 999) and Gas Safe Register · [4] National Poisons Information Service (TOXBASE) · [5] Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm (England) Regulations 2015, amended 2022; Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998
knowledge.summary: Headache, nausea, dizziness and tiredness in several people and a pet in the same home, worse at home and better away, is carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. The first job is to get everyone out and call the gas emergency line; the second is urgent medical assessment, where normal pulse oximetry must not reassure.

points.t: UKHSA [1]: common symptoms are headache, tiredness, difficulty thinking clearly and feeling sick; others include dizziness, drowsiness, chest pain and vomiting. The clues are clustering (several household members, pets affected), timing (worse at home, mornings or when heating is on) and relief away from the house. It is often mislabelled as a virus, migraine or food poisoning.

Ask about gas boilers, fires and cookers, solid-fuel or wood burners, blocked flues or chimneys, recent building work that reduced ventilation, and portable generators or barbecues indoors. Ask whether there is a CO alarm and when appliances were last serviced.

UKHSA [1]: leave the building and get into fresh air, switch off fuel-burning appliances and open windows on the way out, and seek urgent medical advice. From outside, call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 [3]. Call 999 if anyone is drowsy, confused, has chest pain or collapses.

Symptomatic people need same-day assessment where carboxyhaemoglobin can be measured (usually the emergency department). High-flow oxygen speeds elimination [2]. Specialist and hyperbaric decisions follow NPIS/TOXBASE advice [4], particularly with loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac features or pregnancy.
Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so saturations can look normal in significant poisoning [2]. A normal home or ambulance SpO2 does not exclude CO.

Carboxyhaemoglobin falls once someone leaves the source and more quickly on oxygen, so a normal level taken late does not exclude exposure; smokers have higher baseline levels [2]. Interpret results in the light of the history.

Fit an audible CO alarm; have fuel-burning appliances and flues checked by a Gas Safe registered engineer [3]; keep vents clear; never use barbecues or generators indoors. In rented homes, landlords must arrange an annual gas safety check and fit CO alarms in rooms with fixed combustion appliances other than gas cookers [5].

No one should return or use the appliance until the gas engineer has made it safe. Delayed neurological effects (memory, concentration, mood) can follow significant exposure; arrange review if these appear [2].

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Toller? I’m Dr Clarke from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth for me? … Thank you. How can I help?
model.why: Identity check on the telephone; open question

model.text: This sounds odd, doctor. For two weeks me, my partner and the two kids have all had headaches, felt sick and dizzy and tired. Even the dog seems off and sleepy. We feel rough at home, especially mornings, but when we’re out for the day we’re fine. Is there a bug going round?
That’s really helpful, and it’s not odd at all. Can I ask straight away: where are you now, and how are you feeling at this moment?
model.why: Recognises the pattern immediately and checks current location

model.text: I’m at home. Headache, a bit woozy.

Mrs Toller, symptoms in everyone at home, even the dog, that are worse in the house and better when you’re out, make me worried about carbon monoxide. It’s a gas you can’t see or smell. Before we go further I want you to act now. Is anyone in the house very sleepy, confused or hard to wake?
model.why: Names possible CO and screens for 999 features first

model.text: No, no one’s like that. Are you serious?

I am, and I’ll explain. Please get everyone who is in the house, and the dog, out into the fresh air now. If it’s on and you can reach it quickly, switch off the boiler or any gas fire, and open windows as you go. Don’t stay inside to do anything else. I’ll stay on the line.
model.why: UKHSA immediate advice: out, switch off, ventilate

model.text: Okay … I’m going out the front now. The dog’s with me.
Good. Once you’re outside, you need to ring the National Gas Emergency number, 0800 111 999. They’ll come and check the house. Have you got that written down or can I text it to you?
model.why: Gas emergency service with number, confirmed

model.text: Text it, please. I’m outside now.
Well done. Now a few questions. What heats the house and what do you cook on? Any gas fire, wood burner or chimney?
It’s an old house. Gas boiler and a gas fire in the lounge. The heating’s been on a lot.
Do you have a carbon monoxide alarm, and do you know when the boiler was last serviced?
I don’t think we’ve got an alarm. I don’t know about the boiler, to be honest.
Has anyone had chest pain, fainting, confusion or being sick a lot? And is anyone in the household pregnant or have a heart or lung problem?
Just headaches and feeling sick. I don’t think so for the rest.
You thought it was a bug. What’s going through your mind now?
I feel awful. I’ve had the kids in there. Have I made them ill?
That’s a very natural worry, but you couldn’t have known. It’s called the silent killer because you can’t see or smell it. Ringing today is exactly what has made them safer.
Okay. What happens now?

Everyone who has symptoms needs checking today at the hospital emergency department, where they can do a blood test that measures carbon monoxide and give oxygen, which clears it faster. I’ll ring ahead and let them know you’re all coming.
model.why: Urgent assessment where carboxyhaemoglobin can be measured; direct handover

model.text: Couldn’t I just check them with one of those finger oxygen monitors?

Good question, but no. Those finger monitors can read normal even when carbon monoxide is high, because they can’t tell the difference. A normal reading won’t tell us you’re safe. And the blood level drops once you’re in fresh air, so please go today rather than waiting.
model.why: Explains falsely normal oximetry and falling COHb

model.text: Right. What about my partner and the kids, if they’re not with me?
Please let them know not to go back into the house, and to come with you to be checked. If any of them feels very drowsy, confused, has chest pain or collapses, call 999.
model.why: Extends advice to all household members with 999 triggers

model.text: When can we go back home?

Only when the gas engineer says it’s safe. Before using the boiler or fire again, a Gas Safe registered engineer needs to check them and the flue, and please fit a carbon monoxide alarm. If you rent, your landlord must arrange the gas safety check and alarm.
model.why: Prevention: Gas Safe, alarms, landlord duty

model.text: Let’s check the plan. Can you tell it back to me?
Stay out. Ring 0800 111 999. Everyone to A&E today to be checked. Don’t trust the finger monitor. 999 if anyone’s drowsy or collapses. Don’t go back in until it’s safe.

Exactly right. Some people get problems with memory, concentration or mood in the weeks after exposure, so if you notice anything like that in any of you, book in with me. I’ll text the number now and ring the hospital. I’ll call you tomorrow to see how you all got on.
model.why: Delayed effects, follow-up call and practical actions

model.text: Thank you. I’m so glad I rang.

social.t: Older homes, blocked vents and unserviced appliances are common sources. Families struggling with energy costs may block vents to keep warm, raising the risk.
Energy suppliers and network operators keep a Priority Services Register; some eligible households can get extra support, including free gas safety checks. Signpost if cost is a barrier.

legal.t: Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998: landlords must arrange an annual gas safety check by a Gas Safe registered engineer. Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm (England) Regulations 2015, amended 2022: CO alarms in rooms with a fixed combustion appliance (excluding gas cookers) in rented homes.
Gas Safe engineers must report certain dangerous gas fittings and incidents under RIDDOR 2013; the GP does not need to report, but should record the suspected source.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise when remote consultation is not enough; here it is not, and the plan must include urgent in-person assessment.
Other family members may be registered at the practice or elsewhere. With consent, note the exposure on their records so later symptoms are interpreted correctly.

community.t: National Gas Emergency Service (0800 111 999) attends suspected leaks and CO. Many fire and rescue services offer home safety visits that include CO advice.

Pets unwell at the same time

Whether she rents or owns (landlord duties)

playbook.diagnosisLay: “Carbon monoxide is a gas made when fuel doesn’t burn properly. It sticks to the blood in place of oxygen, so the body is short of oxygen even though you’re breathing normally. You can’t see or smell it.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was a bug, and it looks like one, but the pattern at home is the clue. You couldn’t have known, and ringing has made everyone safer.”

pitfalls.intro: The trap is answering her question about a bug. The marks sit in spotting the household pattern, acting while she is still inside, and not being fooled by normal oximetry.

items.why: Several people and a pet, worse at home and better away, is the carbon monoxide pattern.
items.fix: Ask “Is it worse at home and better when you’re out?” and act on the answer.

items.fail: Taking a full history before telling her to leave.
items.fix: Get her and the household out first, then ask the questions.

items.why: The source must be made safe; UKHSA and Gas Safe advice is to call the emergency line.
items.fix: Give 0800 111 999 and offer to text it.

items.fail: Accepting a normal finger oximeter reading.
items.fix: Same-day assessment where a blood level can be measured.

items.fail: Ignoring her guilt about the children.
items.why: It is her hidden concern and affects how she hears the plan.
items.fix: “You couldn’t have known. Ringing today made them safer.”

items.fail: No plan for returning home or prevention.
items.why: Returning to an unserviced appliance repeats the exposure.
items.fix: No return until declared safe; Gas Safe check; CO alarm; landlord duty if rented.

The first job is to get everyone out and call the gas emergency line; the second is urgent medical assessment, where normal pulse oximetry must not reassure.

points.t: UKHSA [1]: common symptoms are headache, tiredness, difficulty thinking clearly and feeling sick; others include dizziness, drowsiness, chest pain and vomiting. The clues are clustering (several household members, pets affected), timing (worse at home, mornings or when heating is on) and relief away from the house. It is often mislabelled as a virus, migraine or food poisoning.

Ask about gas boilers, fires and cookers, solid-fuel or wood burners, blocked flues or chimneys, recent building work that reduced ventilation, and portable generators or barbecues indoors. Ask whether there is a CO alarm and when appliances were last serviced.

UKHSA [1]: leave the building and get into fresh air, switch off fuel-burning appliances and open windows on the way out, and seek urgent medical advice. From outside, call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 [3]. Call 999 if anyone is drowsy, confused, has chest pain or collapses.

Symptomatic people need same-day assessment where carboxyhaemoglobin can be measured (usually the emergency department). High-flow oxygen speeds elimination [2]. Specialist and hyperbaric decisions follow NPIS/TOXBASE advice [4], particularly with loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac features or pregnancy.
Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so saturations can look normal in significant poisoning [2]. A normal home or ambulance SpO2 does not exclude CO.

Carboxyhaemoglobin falls once someone leaves the source and more quickly on oxygen, so a normal level taken late does not exclude exposure; smokers have higher baseline levels [2]. Interpret results in the light of the history.

Fit an audible CO alarm; have fuel-burning appliances and flues checked by a Gas Safe registered engineer [3]; keep vents clear; never use barbecues or generators indoors. In rented homes, landlords must arrange an annual gas safety check and fit CO alarms in rooms with fixed combustion appliances other than gas cookers [5].

No one should return or use the appliance until the gas engineer has made it safe. Delayed neurological effects (memory, concentration, mood) can follow significant exposure; arrange review if these appear [2].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; listened to the whole household pattern before asking; checked identity on the phone.
Home heating and housing; who is in the house; guilt about the children; ability to leave and get to hospital.
Picked up “even the dog”, “worse at home” and “fine when we’re out” as the diagnostic clue.
Idea (a bug going round), concern (guilt about having the children in the house), expectation (reassurance about a virus).
Recognised that a telephone call cannot assess this; same-day ED assessment for carboxyhaemoglobin; oximetry explained as unreliable.
Carbon monoxide poisoning versus viral illness, migraine, food poisoning.
Screened drowsiness, confusion, chest pain, collapse, pregnancy and cardiorespiratory disease; gave 999 criteria.
Suspected carbon monoxide poisoning from a domestic gas appliance.
Immediate evacuation, appliances off, windows open, 0800 111 999; ED assessment with oxygen; Gas Safe check and CO alarm before return.
Advice extended to all household members; landlord duties if rented; delayed neurological effects mentioned.
Teach-back; number texted; hospital phoned ahead; follow-up call next day.

social.t: Older homes, blocked vents and unserviced appliances are common sources. Families struggling with energy costs may block vents to keep warm, raising the risk.
Energy suppliers and network operators keep a Priority Services Register; some eligible households can get extra support, including free gas safety checks. Signpost if cost is a barrier.

legal.t: Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998: landlords must arrange an annual gas safety check by a Gas Safe registered engineer. Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm (England) Regulations 2015, amended 2022: CO alarms in rooms with a fixed combustion appliance (excluding gas cookers) in rented homes.
Gas Safe engineers must report certain dangerous gas fittings and incidents under RIDDOR 2013; the GP does not need to report, but should record the suspected source.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise when remote consultation is not enough; here it is not, and the plan must include urgent in-person assessment.
Other family members may be registered at the practice or elsewhere. With consent, note the exposure on their records so later symptoms are interpreted correctly.

community.t: National Gas Emergency Service (0800 111 999) attends suspected leaks and CO. Many fire and rescue services offer home safety visits that include CO advice.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Headaches, sickness and dizziness in everyone at home, even the dog, worse in the house and better when you’re out, point to carbon monoxide from a faulty appliance.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Carbon monoxide is a gas made when fuel doesn’t burn properly. It sticks to the blood in place of oxygen, so the body is short of oxygen even though you’re breathing normally. You can’t see or smell it.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was a bug, and it looks like one, but the pattern at home is the clue. You couldn’t have known, and ringing has made everyone safer.”
management.psychosocial: Address guilt; check she can get everyone to hospital; landlord or cost barriers to servicing; Priority Services Register if relevant.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is answering her question about a bug. The marks sit in spotting the household pattern, acting while she is still inside, and not being fooled by normal oximetry.

items.why: Several people and a pet, worse at home and better away, is the carbon monoxide pattern.
items.fix: Ask “Is it worse at home and better when you’re out?” and act on the answer.

items.fail: Taking a full history before telling her to leave.
items.fix: Get her and the household out first, then ask the questions.

items.why: The source must be made safe; UKHSA and Gas Safe advice is to call the emergency line.
items.fix: Give 0800 111 999 and offer to text it.

items.fail: Accepting a normal finger oximeter reading.
items.fix: Same-day assessment where a blood level can be measured.

items.fail: Ignoring her guilt about the children.
items.why: It is her hidden concern and affects how she hears the plan.
items.fix: “You couldn’t have known. Ringing today made them safer.”

items.fail: No plan for returning home or prevention.
items.why: Returning to an unserviced appliance repeats the exposure.
items.fix: No return until declared safe; Gas Safe check; CO alarm; landlord duty if rented.
